claim: Microtubules are nucleated from specific locations at precise times in the cell cycle.
source: Microtubules are nucleated from specific locations at precise times in the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a general statement about microtubule biology presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Branching microtubule nucleation is critical for chromosome segregation.
source: Using purified Xenopus laevis proteins we biochemically reconstitute branching microtubule nucleation, which is critical for chromosome segregation.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: γ-TuRC, augmin, and TPX2 are required to efficiently nucleate microtubules from pre-existing microtubules.
source: We found that besides the microtubule nucleator gamma-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC), the branching effectors augmin and TPX2 are required to efficiently nucleate microtubules from pre-existing microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by the reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 3E where all three factors together produce the highest level of branching microtubule nucleation.

claim: TPX2 has the capacity to directly recruit γ-TuRC.
source: TPX2 has the unexpected capacity to directly recruit γ-TuRC as well as augmin, which in turn targets more γ-TuRC along the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is supported by the binding experiments shown in Figure 2B-C where TPX2 alone marginally increases γ-TuRC binding to microtubules.

claim: TPX2 can directly recruit augmin to microtubules.
source: TPX2 has the unexpected capacity to directly recruit γ-TuRC as well as augmin, which in turn targets more γ-TuRC along the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is supported by the sequential binding experiments in Figure 2E-F showing that microtubule-bound TPX2 increases the amount of augmin bound to the microtubule.

claim: Augmin targets γ-TuRC along the microtubule lattice.
source: TPX2 has the unexpected capacity to directly recruit γ-TuRC as well as augmin, which in turn targets more γ-TuRC along the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B-C showing that augmin increases γ-TuRC binding to microtubules.

claim: TPX2 and augmin enable γ-TuRC-dependent microtubule nucleation at preferred branching angles of less than 90 degrees.
source: TPX2 and augmin enable γ-TuRC-dependent microtubule nucleation at preferred branching angles of less than 90 degrees from regularly-spaced patches along microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by the branching angle measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Branching microtubule nucleation occurs from regularly-spaced patches along microtubules.
source: TPX2 and augmin enable γ-TuRC-dependent microtubule nucleation at preferred branching angles of less than 90 degrees from regularly-spaced patches along microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy images in Figure 2D and fluorescence microscopy in Figure 3D showing distinct puncta along microtubules.

claim: Microtubules in cells are nucleated by γ-TuRC.
source: Importantly, microtubules in cells are nucleated by the microtubule nucleator γ-TuRC (Kollman et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 1995) and its co-nucleation factor XMAP215 (Flor-Parra et al., 2018; Gunzelmann et al., 2018; Thawani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: XMAP215 is a co-nucleation factor for γ-TuRC.
source: Importantly, microtubules in cells are nucleated by the microtubule nucleator γ-TuRC (Kollman et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 1995) and its co-nucleation factor XMAP215 (Flor-Parra et al., 2018; Gunzelmann et al., 2018; Thawani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Each microtubule nucleation pathway requires a unique set of nucleation effectors to recruit and regulate γ-TuRC at distinct cellular locations.
source: At the same time, each microtubule nucleation pathway requires a unique set of nucleation effectors to recruit and regulate γ-TuRC at distinct cellular locations (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Branching microtubule nucleation amplifies microtubule number while preserving their polarity.
source: Microtubules can nucleate from pre-existing microtubules, termed branching microtubule nucleation (Petry et al., 2013), which amplifies microtubule number while preserving their polarity, as is needed in the mitotic spindle and in axons (Cunha-Ferreira et al., 2018; David et al., 2019; Kamasaki et al., 2013; Petry et al., 2013; Sánchez-Huertas et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Augmin is required for branching microtubule nucleation in plant, human and Drosophila cells, and meiotic Xenopus egg extract.
source: The eight-subunit protein complex augmin is required for branching microtubule nucleation in plant, human and Drosophila cells, and meiotic Xenopus egg extract, where its depletion leads to reduced spindle microtubule density, less kinetochore fiber tension, metaphase arrest, and cytokinesis failure (David et al., 2019; Decker et al., 2018; Goshima et al., 2008; Hayward et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2011; Kamasaki et al., 2013; Lawo et al., 2009; Nakaoka et al., 2012; Petry et al., 2011; Uehara et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Augmin depletion leads to reduced spindle microtubule density, less kinetochore fiber tension, metaphase arrest, and cytokinesis failure.
source: The eight-subunit protein complex augmin is required for branching microtubule nucleation in plant, human and Drosophila cells, and meiotic Xenopus egg extract, where its depletion leads to reduced spindle microtubule density, less kinetochore fiber tension, metaphase arrest, and cytokinesis failure (David et al., 2019; Decker et al., 2018; Goshima et al., 2008; Hayward et al., 2014; Ho et al., 2011; Kamasaki et al., 2013; Lawo et al., 2009; Nakaoka et al., 2012; Petry et al., 2011; Uehara et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Augmin is necessary to recruit γ-TuRC to spindle microtubules.
source: Augmin is necessary to recruit γ-TuRC to spindle microtubules (Goshima et al., 2007), and following the recombinant expression of augmin (Hsia et al., 2014), this activity was confirmed using purified proteins (Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TPX2 is released near chromatin in meiotic Xenopus egg extract.
source: In meiotic Xenopus egg extract, the Ran-regulated protein TPX2 is released near chromatin (Gruss et al., 2001), where it stimulates branching microtubule nucleation (Petry et al., 2013), potentially by activating γ-TuRC via nucleation activator motifs (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TPX2 stimulates branching microtubule nucleation near chromatin.
source: In meiotic Xenopus egg extract, the Ran-regulated protein TPX2 is released near chromatin (Gruss et al., 2001), where it stimulates branching microtubule nucleation (Petry et al., 2013), potentially by activating γ-TuRC via nucleation activator motifs (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TPX2 potentially activates γ-TuRC via nucleation activator motifs.
source: In meiotic Xenopus egg extract, the Ran-regulated protein TPX2 is released near chromatin (Gruss et al., 2001), where it stimulates branching microtubule nucleation (Petry et al., 2013), potentially by activating γ-TuRC via nucleation activator motifs (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is presented as a possibility supported by a citation, indicating speculation based on previous work.

claim: TPX2 forms a co-condensate with tubulin along the microtubule lattice, which enhances the kinetic efficiency of branching microtubule nucleation.
source: Recently, TPX2 was also observed to form a co-condensate with tubulin along the microtubule lattice, which enhances the kinetic efficiency of branching microtubule nucleation (King and Petry, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In meiotic Xenopus egg extract, TPX2 needs to bind to microtubules before augmin/γ-TuRC to result in a successful nucleation event.
source: In meiotic Xenopus egg extract, TPX2 needs to bind to microtubules before augmin/γ-TuRC to result in a successful nucleation event (Thawani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In mitotic Drosophila cells TPX2 is not required, and augmin can bind to microtubules before γ-TuRC.
source: In contrast, in mitotic Drosophila cells TPX2 is not required, and augmin can bind to microtubules before γ-TuRC (Verma and Maresca, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: An endogenous, pre-existing microtubule can serve as a template for branching microtubule nucleation when exposed to Ran-supplemented extract.
source: Using multicolor time-lapse total internal reflection (TIRF) microscopy, we first confirmed that an endogenous, pre-existing microtubule can serve as a template for branching microtubule nucleation when exposed to Ran-supplemented extract that releases branching factors (Figure 1A and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A microtubule formed independent of Ran can serve as the site for binding of branching factors and subsequent nucleation events.
source: This shows that a microtubule formed independent of Ran can serve as the site for binding of branching factors and subsequent nucleation events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All necessary Ran-regulated branching factors bind to the pre-existing microtubule prior to microtubule nucleation.
source: To gain mechanistic insight, we hypothesized that all necessary Ran-regulated branching factors bind to the pre-existing microtubule prior to microtubule nucleation.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis that was then tested experimentally.

claim: Ran-regulated branching factors bind to microtubules independent of their successful nucleation reactions.
source: When another extract reaction was subsequently added, new microtubules nucleated almost exclusively from pre-existing microtubules, indicating that Ran-regulated branching factors bind to microtubules independent of their successful nucleation reactions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Upon binding of branching factors and γ-TuRC, tubulin is the only protein required to form new branched microtubules from the localized factors.
source: Surprisingly, short branched microtubules nucleated from pre-existing microtubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), showing that upon binding of branching factors and γ-TuRC, tubulin is the only protein required to form new branched microtubules from the localized factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Branched microtubules retain the polarity of the pre-existing microtubule.
source: This revealed that branched microtubules retained the polarity of the pre-existing microtubule, and new microtubules do not appear to nucleate from other branched microtubules, suggesting that the branching factors do not relocate between microtubules (Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: New microtubules do not appear to nucleate from other branched microtubules.
source: This revealed that branched microtubules retained the polarity of the pre-existing microtubule, and new microtubules do not appear to nucleate from other branched microtubules, suggesting that the branching factors do not relocate between microtubules (Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Branching factors do not relocate between microtubules.
source: This revealed that branched microtubules retained the polarity of the pre-existing microtubule, and new microtubules do not appear to nucleate from other branched microtubules, suggesting that the branching factors do not relocate between microtubules (Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that new microtubules do not nucleate from other branched microtubules.

claim: The deposition of branching factors and γ-TuRC to the pre-existing microtubule determines branching architecture.
source: Thus, solely the deposition of branching factors and γ-TuRC to the pre-existing microtubule determines branching architecture.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in Figure 1.

claim: Purified γ-TuRC, when tethered along the microtubule lattice via artificial linkers, can nucleate microtubules.
source: Because the key for branching microtubule nucleation is to target γ-TuRC along the length of a microtubule, we verified as a proof of concept that purified γ-TuRC, when tethered along the microtubule lattice via artificial linkers, can still nucleate microtubules, which indeed was the case (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: γ-TuRC binds along the length of microtubules in the presence of augmin.
source: γ-TuRC, visualized by a fluorescently-labeled antibody, bound along the length of microtubules in the presence of augmin (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—source data 1) consistent with previous studies (Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–C and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: TPX2 alone marginally increases the binding of γ-TuRC to microtubules compared to non-specific γ-TuRC binding.
source: Unexpectedly, TPX2 alone marginally increased the binding of γ-TuRC to microtubules compared to non-specific γ-TuRC binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: A higher amount of γ-TuRC is recruited all along the microtubule lattice in the presence of both TPX2 and augmin.
source: A higher amount of γ-TuRC was recruited all along the microtubule lattice in the presence of both TPX2 and augmin (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: Augmin and TPX2 form distinct puncta on microtubules, where γ-TuRC is recruited.
source: Surprisingly, augmin and TPX2 formed distinct puncta on microtubules, where γ-TuRC was recruited.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in Figure 2B and Figure 3D.

claim: γ-TuRC is recruited to regularly spaced patches along microtubules where it accumulates.
source: Using negative stain electron microscopy, we visualized this binding at higher resolution and indeed observed that γ-TuRC is recruited to regularly spaced patches, where it accumulates (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Microtubule-bound TPX2 increases the amount of augmin bound to the microtubule.
source: Surprisingly, microtubule-bound TPX2 increased the amount of augmin bound to the microtubule, whereas the presence of augmin did not change the level of bound TPX2 (Figure 2E–F and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: The presence of augmin does not change the level of bound TPX2.
source: Surprisingly, microtubule-bound TPX2 increased the amount of augmin bound to the microtubule, whereas the presence of augmin did not change the level of bound TPX2 (Figure 2E–F and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: Branching microtubule nucleation from a template microtubule occurs using only purified TPX2, augmin, and γ-TuRC.
source: Remarkably, branching microtubule nucleation from a template microtubule occurred using only purified proteins (Figure 3B and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TPX2, augmin and γ-TuRC are sufficient to specifically nucleate new branched microtubules, which remain attached at the nucleation site on the template microtubule.
source: Thus, TPX2, augmin and γ-TuRC are sufficient to specifically nucleate new branched microtubules, which remain attached at the nucleation site on the template microtubule (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: New microtubules nucleate all along the template microtubule without any preference for the template's plus- or minus-ends.
source: New microtubules nucleate all along the template microtubule without any preference for the template's plus- or minus-ends (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1), likely because the template microtubule was fully available for simultaneous binding of branching factors in our assay set-up.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is no signature on the stabilized microtubule lattice that determines where a branch occurs.
source: Thus, there is no signature on the stabilized microtubule lattice that determines where a branch occurs, only that microtubule nucleation events occur from distinct TPX2/augmin puncta distributed along the microtubule lattice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that branches occur uniformly along the microtubule without preference for ends.

claim: Microtubule nucleation events occur from distinct TPX2/augmin puncta distributed along the microtubule lattice.
source: Thus, there is no signature on the stabilized microtubule lattice that determines where a branch occurs, only that microtubule nucleation events occur from distinct TPX2/augmin puncta distributed along the microtubule lattice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Multiple microtubules can be generated from the same puncta as resolved by light microscopy.
source: Multiple microtubules can be generated from the same puncta as resolved by light microscopy (Figure 3D), which presumably nucleate from neighboring γ-TuRCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in Figure 3D.

claim: Multiple microtubules from the same puncta presumably nucleate from neighboring γ-TuRCs.
source: Multiple microtubules can be generated from the same puncta as resolved by light microscopy (Figure 3D), which presumably nucleate from neighboring γ-TuRCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the electron microscopy data showing multiple γ-TuRCs in patches (Figure 2D).

claim: γ-TuRC is essential for branching microtubule nucleation.
source: Notably, γ-TuRC is essential for branching microtubule nucleation (Figure 3E and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E where no branching occurs without γ-TuRC.

claim: TPX2 alone or together with augmin cannot nucleate branched microtubules.
source: Despite the fact that TPX2 can recruit tubulin (King and Petry, 2019), it alone or together with augmin cannot nucleate branched microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and a citation to previous work.

claim: γ-TuRC can infrequently bind to the microtubule lattice on its own.
source: γ-TuRC can infrequently bind to the microtubule lattice on its own (Figure 2D), leading to rare nucleation events without TPX2 and augmin (Figure 3E and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 3E.

claim: Augmin and γ-TuRC can cause branching microtubule nucleation to a limited extent.
source: Not surprisingly, augmin and γ-TuRC can cause branching microtubule nucleation to a limited extent (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C and Figure 3—source data 2), as augmin can directly recruit γ-TuRC to a pre-existing microtubule in vitro (Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C, and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: TPX2 and γ-TuRC can cause branching microtubule nucleation to a similar extent as augmin and γ-TuRC.
source: Surprisingly, TPX2 and γ-TuRC can also cause branching microtubule nucleation to a similar extent as augmin and γ-TuRC (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E.

claim: Only when augmin, TPX2 and γ-TuRC are present, branching microtubule nucleation occurs most often.
source: Importantly, only when augmin, TPX2 and γ-TuRC are present, branching microtubule nucleation occurs most often (Figure 3E and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Branched microtubules are preferentially formed in angles < 90 degrees, with 0–15 degrees being the most common.
source: Branched microtubules are preferentially formed in angles < 90 degrees, with 0–15 degrees being the most common (Figure 3F and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Most branched microtubules maintain the same polarity as the mother microtubule.
source: This way, most branched microtubules maintain the same polarity as the mother microtubule, a hallmark of branching microtubule nucleation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that most branches form at angles < 90 degrees.

claim: The angle of microtubule branches did not drastically change when augmin or TPX2 were combined with γ-TuRC.
source: The angle of microtubule branches did not drastically change when augmin or TPX2 were combined with γ-TuRC, only that augmin/γ-TuRC alone caused a higher proportion of shallow branch angles (Figure 3F and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Augmin/γ-TuRC alone causes a higher proportion of shallow branch angles.
source: The angle of microtubule branches did not drastically change when augmin or TPX2 were combined with γ-TuRC, only that augmin/γ-TuRC alone caused a higher proportion of shallow branch angles (Figure 3F and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The addition of TPX2 or augmin does not change the number of non-branched microtubules.
source: Reactions where γ-TuRC was present have approximately twice as many non-branched microtubules per field of view compared to the reactions where γ-TuRC was absent. Notably, the addition of TPX2 or augmin does not change the number of non-branched microtubules (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and Figure 3—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The increase in branching microtubule nucleation by TPX2 and augmin is not just a result of increased microtubule nucleation overall, but specifically occurs from a pre-existing microtubule.
source: This suggests that the increase in branching microtubule nucleation by TPX2 and augmin is not just a result of increased microtubule nucleation overall, but specifically occurs from a pre-existing microtubule.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that TPX2 and augmin do not increase non-branched microtubule nucleation.

claim: Augmin does not enhance the nucleation activity of purified γ-TuRC in vitro.
source: Augmin did not enhance the nucleation activity of purified γ-TuRC in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), consistent with previous studies (Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: A low concentration of TPX2 (10 nM) does not enhance the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC.
source: A low concentration of TPX2 (10 nM) did not enhance the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC either (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: At 50 nM concentration and in the absence of pre-formed microtubules, TPX2 forms co-condensates with tubulin in solution that nucleate microtubules in vitro.
source: A higher concentration of TPX2 (50 nM) was also tested, but at this concentration and in the absence of pre-formed microtubules, TPX2 forms co-condensates with tubulin in solution that nucleate microtubules in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D) (King and Petry, 2019), which precludes the accurate assessment of γ-TuRC-mediated microtubule nucleation at higher concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and a citation to previous work.

claim: TPX2 and augmin do not activate γ-TuRC in solution.
source: These nucleation experiments suggest that TPX2 and augmin do not activate γ-TuRC in solution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the nucleation experiments in solution shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: XMAP215 co-localizes to the template microtubule and appears to increase both microtubule nucleation rate and length.
source: Indeed, XMAP215 co-localizes to the template microtubule and appears to increase both microtubule nucleation rate and length (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Only when TPX2 was bound first and augmin/γ-TuRC second, a higher level of branching microtubule nucleation was measured.
source: Indeed, only when TPX2 was bound first and augmin/γ-TuRC second, a higher level of branching microtubule nucleation was measured (Figure 3G and Figure 3—source data 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The three factors TPX2, augmin and γ-TuRC are sufficient to cause branching microtubule nucleation.
source: Via an in vitro reconstitution, we demonstrate that the three factors TPX2, augmin and γ-TuRC are sufficient to cause branching microtubule nucleation and defined the roles of each protein.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the reconstitution experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: γ-TuRC is required for physiological microtubule nucleation.
source: Although microtubule nucleation effectors alone, both as monomers or as phase-separated entities, can generate microtubules in vitro (Roostalu et al., 2015; Woodruff et al., 2017; King and Petry, 2019), γ-TuRC is required for physiological microtubule nucleation (Kollman et al., 2011; Thawani et al., 2018), and this reconstitution highlights the importance of including it when studying microtubule nucleation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microtubule nucleation effectors alone, both as monomers or as phase-separated entities, can generate microtubules in vitro.
source: Although microtubule nucleation effectors alone, both as monomers or as phase-separated entities, can generate microtubules in vitro (Roostalu et al., 2015; Woodruff et al., 2017; King and Petry, 2019), γ-TuRC is required for physiological microtubule nucleation (Kollman et al., 2011; Thawani et al., 2018), and this reconstitution highlights the importance of including it when studying microtubule nucleation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: γ-TuRC's activity can be tuned via the tubulin concentration and the presence of XMAP215.
source: In our in vitro system, γ-TuRC's activity could be tuned via the tubulin concentration and the presence of XMAP215.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The microtubule nucleation capacity of γ-TuRC was not enhanced by TPX2 or augmin in solution.
source: The microtubule nucleation capacity of γ-TuRC was not enhanced by TPX2 or augmin in solution, but these factors specifically enable γ-TuRC-dependent microtubule nucleation from a pre-existing microtubule.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the nucleation assays in solution and on microtubules.

claim: TPX2 and augmin specifically enable γ-TuRC-dependent microtubule nucleation from a pre-existing microtubule.
source: The microtubule nucleation capacity of γ-TuRC was not enhanced by TPX2 or augmin in solution, but these factors specifically enable γ-TuRC-dependent microtubule nucleation from a pre-existing microtubule.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the nucleation assays.

claim: TPX2 and augmin may act as localization factors.
source: This can be explained if TPX2 and augmin act as localization factors, but there is also the possibility that they increase the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC specifically when bound to a microtubule.
evidence: This is presented as a possible explanation for the experimental observations.

claim: TPX2 and augmin may increase the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC specifically when bound to a microtubule.
source: This can be explained if TPX2 and augmin act as localization factors, but there is also the possibility that they increase the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC specifically when bound to a microtubule.
evidence: This is presented as a possible explanation for the experimental observations.

claim: Augmin can recruit γ-TuRC to the side of a pre-existing microtubule, which can subsequently nucleate branched microtubules.
source: Augmin can recruit γ-TuRC to the side of a pre-existing microtubule (Song et al., 2018), which can subsequently nucleate branched microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and the experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: TPX2 increases γ-TuRC localization to microtubules to a small extent.
source: This could be explained by our observation that TPX2 increases γ-TuRC localization to microtubules to a small extent.
evidence: This refers to the experimental observations in Figure 2B-C.

claim: TPX2 can recruit tubulin to the lattice of a pre-existing microtubule by forming a co-condensate.
source: Additionally, it was recently shown that TPX2 can recruit tubulin to the lattice of a pre-existing microtubule by forming a co-condensate (King and Petry, 2019), potentially making lattice-bound γ-TuRC more likely to nucleate branched microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TPX2 contains γ-TuRC activator motifs that have been proposed to activate γ-TuRC.
source: Finally, TPX2 contains γ-TuRC activator motifs that have been proposed to activate γ-TuRC (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TPX2 additionally recruits more augmin, which in turn can localize more γ-TuRC.
source: Besides operating via these three modes in the full reconstitution, TPX2 additionally recruits more augmin, which in turn can localize more γ-TuRC.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 2E-F showing TPX2 recruits augmin.

claim: TPX2 alone creates a slightly wider angle distribution of branches than augmin alone and both factors together.
source: Finally, TPX2 alone creates a slightly wider angle distribution of branches, than augmin alone and both factors together.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 3F.

claim: By bridging the microtubule and γ-TuRC with a defined architecture based on its h-shaped structure, augmin may keep the angle variation in a more shallow range.
source: Thus, by bridging the microtubule and γ-TuRC with a defined architecture based on its h-shaped structure (Hsia et al., 2014; Song et al., 2018), augmin may keep the angle variation in a more shallow range, which is critical for creating parallel structures that retain microtubule polarity as is necessary in the spindle and axons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the experimental observations and citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Both TPX2 and augmin are required in Xenopus egg extract for branching microtubule nucleation.
source: Although TPX2 + γ-TuRC or augmin + γ-TuRC can nucleate microtubules from a pre-existing microtubule in this purified system, both factors are required in Xenopus egg extract for branching microtubule nucleation (Petry et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Microtubule nucleation in a physiological environment is more stringently regulated than in the purified in vitro system.
source: This indicates that microtubule nucleation in a physiological environment is more stringently regulated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between the in vitro system and egg extract results.

claim: TPX2 binding to microtubules is absolutely necessary for augmin/γ-TuRC binding and subsequent branching microtubule nucleation in Xenopus egg extract.
source: Another important difference is that while it is beneficial that TPX2 binds to microtubules before augmin in our in vitro reconstitution, TPX2 binding to microtubules is absolutely necessary for augmin/γ-TuRC binding and subsequent branching microtubule nucleation in Xenopus egg extract (Thawani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TPX2 directly regulates augmin's binding to microtubules in Xenopus egg extract.
source: This implies that TPX2 directly regulates augmin's binding to microtubules in Xenopus egg extract, in a manner that still needs to be uncovered.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison between the in vitro system and egg extract results.

claim: TPX2 lies at the very heart of controlling branching microtubule nucleation.
source: Surprisingly, TPX2, despite being only a single protein amongst large multi-subunit complexes, lies at the very heart of controlling this reaction, as demonstrated in this purified in vitro system and in Xenopus egg extract (Thawani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in this manuscript and previous work.

claim: Other proteins besides TPX2, augmin and γ-TuRC may be involved in additional regulation of branching microtubule nucleation, such as EML3.
source: Finally, even though TPX2, augmin and γ-TuRC are sufficient to reconstitute the nucleation of branched microtubules in vitro, we cannot eliminate the possibility that other proteins are involved in additional regulation, such as the microtubule and augmin binding protein EML3 (Luo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is presented as a possibility with a citation to previous literature.

claim: This work is analogous to the in vitro reconstitution of actin branching, which paved the way to explain how the actin cytoskeleton supports cell locomotion.
source: It is analogous to the in vitro reconstitution of actin branching (Mullins et al., 1998), which paved the way to explain how the actin cytoskeleton supports cell locomotion.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work in the actin field, supported by a citation.

claim: In this biochemical reconstitution, γ-TuRC was localized to a specific location, from which it nucleates a microtubule in vitro as it would occur in the cell.
